title: Google's TPUv8s for Training and Inference at Hot Chips 2026
gist: At Hot Chips 2026 Google detailed its eighth-generation TPU family — the training-focused TPU 8t and inference-focused TPU 8i, shipped together in a single year instead of alternating — pairing 8i with in-house Axion Arm CPUs at 2:1 (displacing x86), and scaling 8t to a 9,600-chip superpod with 2PB shared HBM, 121 EFLOPS of FP4, and roughly 2x the perf-per-watt of TPUv7 Ironwood.

themes.theme: Full-stack custom silicon as hyperscaler moat

insights.claim: Google is the only hyperscaler building custom silicon for both AI training and inference, while other cloud operators develop inference-only chips and rely on commodity (merchant GPU) hardware for training — an accumulated-experience edge Google explicitly cites.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Google is the hyperscaler least dependent on Nvidia for training capacity; watch its capex mix and TPU cloud uptake as a hedge against merchant-GPU pricing.
insights.quote: Whereas the other operators have been focused solely on developing inference hardware while relying on commodity hardware for training, Google has continued to develop their own hardware for both tasks right up to the current day.

insights.claim: With TPUv8, Google is shipping two chips (8t training, 8i inference) in a single year rather than alternating generations, because MoE models create communication/network bottlenecks that raw FLOPS scaling cannot solve — forcing workload-specialized designs.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Accelerator differentiation is shifting from FLOPS to networking/memory; favors interconnect, optics, and HBM suppliers over pure compute plays.
insights.quote: MoE in particular imposes new bottlenecks, as it involves a lot more in the way of communication/network traffic than earlier models. Scaling up FLOPS is not enough.
insights.locator: What’s new in the eighth-gen TPUs?

insights.claim: Google has increased TPU performance a million-fold across eight generations, and is now designing TPUs for external cloud-customer workloads rather than purely internal ones.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Signals Google's intent to commercialize TPUs more aggressively as a merchant-adjacent cloud offering, a competitive threat to Nvidia-based cloud instances.
insights.quote: At this point Google is also designing these chips to build for the world.

insights.claim: Google deliberately builds a training-optimized chip because dark silicon from a compromise design wastes die area and power budget — while, per the presentation, no one else wants to take on optimized training hardware.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Training silicon remains a defensible niche with little hyperscaler competition; Google's Ironwood already has external customers, so TPU training revenue can compound.
insights.quote: No one wants to build an optimized training solution. Training is hard, and Google wants to take it on.
insights.locator: Now shifting gears to the training

themes.theme: TPU 8i inference architecture and the Axion/x86 switch

insights.claim: Google pairs TPU 8i inference chips with its in-house Axion Arm CPUs at a 2-to-1 ratio per node, replacing the x86 CPUs used previously — vertically integrating the host CPU and moving inference nodes off x86 entirely.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Direct socket loss for x86 CPU vendors in Google's AI inference fleet; supports the Arm-in-datacenter thesis and Arm royalty growth.
insights.quote: TPU 8i chips are paired with Axion CPUs in a 2-to-1 ratio inside Google’s nodes. Previously, the company was using x86 CPUs for this task.
insights.locator: Besides providing their own internal chip

insights.claim: Inference chips need more HBM per unit of compute and a higher SRAM-to-compute ratio than training chips — counterintuitively, Google's larger 8-HBM-stack die is the inference chip (8i) while the smaller 6-stack die is the training chip (8t).
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: The inference buildout is disproportionately an HBM and on-die memory demand story — bullish for memory suppliers relative to logic-only exposure.
insights.quote: But the point is that inference needs more HBM per unit of compute. Inference also needs a higher percentage of SRAM to compute.
insights.locator: Now for a brief audience participation

insights.claim: Inference cost rises sharply as latency targets tighten — throughput drops with higher per-user token rates — so Google loaded the 8i with more SRAM, more memory, and more bandwidth to bend that cost curve.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Low-latency (agentic, interactive) inference is the expensive tier; whoever cuts cost-per-token at low latency wins pricing power in AI serving.
insights.quote: Looking at the cost of inference, the price goes up quickly the lower the latency is.
insights.locator: Looking at the cost of inference

insights.claim: For inference, Google replaced its 3D Torus interconnect with the BoardFly topology (8 trays of 4 TPUs, 36 groups) that caps worst-case at 7 network hops versus 16 for the torus, because fly networks' lower latency matters more for inference than torus bandwidth patterns suited to training.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Network topology is now workload-specific inside hyperscalers; interconnect innovation is a live differentiator, not settled infrastructure.
insights.quote: The BoardFly network for 8i has a maximum of 7 hops, versus 16 hops for the torus.

insights.claim: TPU 8i offloads in-network collective operations into the ICI I/O die at the chip edge next to the networking hardware, eliminating both the data transfer to the compute die and the associated HBM accesses.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Compute is migrating into the network/I-O path; validates in-network compute (DPU/switch-offload) approaches across the accelerator industry.

themes.theme: TPU 8t training scale and the Virgo fabric

insights.claim: Google's TPU 8t superpod scales to 9,600 chips with an aggregate 2PB of shared HBM and 121 EFLOPS of FP4 compute, arranged as 300 racks with 4 TPUs per tray, delivering roughly 2x the perf-per-watt of TPUv7 Ironwood.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A concrete benchmark for hyperscaler training density and efficiency; use it to gauge how competitive Google's cost-per-training-FLOP is versus Nvidia-based clusters.
insights.quote: the 8t superpod will have 9600 chips, with access to an aggregate 2PB of shared HBM memory. In terms of compute, this is 121 EFLOPS of FP4 compute.

insights.claim: Google's 2x perf-per-watt gain in TPU 8t comes not from FP4 alone but from efficiently handling mixed-precision training recipes, since not all training functions map to FP4.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Headline FP4 FLOPS numbers across the industry overstate usable training performance; mixed-precision handling is the real efficiency lever to scrutinize in vendor claims.
insights.quote: Not all functions map to FP4, however.
insights.locator: Not all functions map to FP4

insights.claim: With TPU 8t Google abandons its general datacenter network for training and introduces the dedicated two-layer Virgo cluster fabric, supporting 134K TPUs in a single domain at 47 Pbits/second of bandwidth.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Dedicated AI back-end fabrics are becoming standard even at Google; sustained demand signal for high-radix switching, optics, and AI-specific networking gear.
insights.quote: This supports 134K TPUs in a single domain, for 47 Pbits/second of bandwidth.

insights.claim: Google's optical circuit switch (OCS) lets the 9,600-chip scale-up domain be dynamically sliced into any size or shape, and handles failures by dropping bad chips, allocating a spare node, and restoring from checkpoint.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Optical circuit switching is a structural Google advantage in cluster utilization and reliability; watch optical switching suppliers as other hyperscalers try to replicate it.

insights.claim: Google architects TPU clusters on the working assumption that chips will be flaky, adding in-field unit testing that runs during idle cycles to detect partial chip failures — treating failure tolerance as a design requirement, not an exception.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: At 100K+ chip scale, RAS and fault-tolerant orchestration become the bottleneck competency; an underappreciated moat for incumbents and a market for reliability tooling.
insights.quote: The working assumption is that the chips will be flaky, so the architecture needs to be able to account for this and work around failed chips.
insights.locator: As always, RAS is a huge

insights.claim: Because semiconductor wear roughly doubles for every 10-15C rise in operating temperature (Arrhenius equation), cooling is a reliability imperative — and TPU 8t is the first generation where Google liquid-cools its optics, not just the chips.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Liquid cooling scope is expanding beyond compute to optics; incremental TAM for datacenter thermal-management suppliers as AI racks densify.
insights.quote: This is the first time that Google is liquid cooling their optics as well. Previously those were air-cooled.

insights.claim: Google used AI models in the design of TPUv8, trimming TPU 8t power consumption and saving die area on both the training and inference chips, which allowed more computational cores to be packed in.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: AI-assisted chip design is delivering measurable PPA gains in production silicon — a recursive-improvement loop that compounds Google's silicon cadence and pressures EDA incumbents to embed AI.
insights.quote: Google is also using AI to help design their TPUs.

insights.claim: Existing TPU codebases run unmodified on TPUv8, while Google's Pallas kernel language lets developers write hardware-aware kernels in Python for peak performance on both 8t and 8i — deepening the software moat around the TPU ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Backward compatibility plus a proprietary kernel path lowers switching costs into TPU and raises them out — a CUDA-style lock-in dynamic worth tracking for TPU cloud adoption.
insights.locator: And briefly on the software front

insights.claim: Google's enduring TPU design philosophy is tight co-design between compiler/software teams and hardware developers so the chip avoids doing any more work than necessary at runtime.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Vertical software-hardware co-design is the core efficiency edge merchant-silicon customers cannot easily match; it underpins Google's claimed cost advantage in AI compute.
insights.quote: employing a strong co-design link between their software (compiler) and hardware developers in order to avoid doing any more than they have to at runtime
